tools.title: An extremely unofficial first look at the 2028 Senate map
tools.summary_raw: Do Republicans have any chance of winning the Senate back? And could Democrats gain a filibuster-proof majority if they have another big night?
tools.content_text: Chuck Grassley, 93, shown here at a campaign event for Ashley Hinson, hasn’t decided whether to run for re-election in 2028. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images. I wasn’t planning to publish anything today, but I had some time on my train down to Washington, where we’ll be doing a live episode of Still Counting tomorrow morning at Crooked Con . Since it’s a mostly progressive audience, we figure we’ll spend most of our time talking about how Democrats might respond in the wake of their extraordinary night . And then we’ll tackle the equally challenging question of how Republicans might try to clean up after their disaster, probably on our regular Wednesday show. Although I have to say that Trump’s decision to replace Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller as his chief of staff isn’t exactly rational behavior given the scope of the Republican defeat. While doing the prep for these shows, though, I found I needed a clearer mental picture of the Senate landscape in 2028. Democrats are probably going to end up with 56 Senate seats this year: prediction markets have Scott Colom and Mary Peltola as 98 percent favorites to eventually be declared the winners in Mississippi (!!!!!) and Alaska, respectively. That’s a lot of Democrats. Other than Sherrod Brown, whose victory came in a special election so he’ll be on the ballot again in 2028, the Democrats elected this year won’t face voters again until 2032. They’ll serve for the entirety of the 48th President’s first term. But having a lot of Democrats comes with a lot of responsibility for the party. So I wanted to get some sense of how large the Democratic majority might (or might not) be in 2029 when the next president is sworn in given three scenarios: Tsunami 2.0. A repeat of Tuesday night, with another D +13 environment on the national House ballot. A good-but-not-great Democratic night. A +5 national environment. Think roughly a climate like 2012, except Democrats realize the environment more efficiently in the House than they did in that election. 1 A modest Republican win. An R +3 House popular vote, roughly like in 2024. On the train, I found myself jotting down a series of provisional race ratings using the categories that groups like Cook Political Report typically use, from “Solid R” to toss-up to “Solid D”. Yes, I’m going to share those ratings. No, you shouldn’t take them all that seriously. Yes, I’m going to put them behind the paywall because it makes it less likely that they’ll be taken out of context. I do not want to overbill or overpromise what these reflect: They are not FLIPR ratings. There is not extensive race-by-race commentary, just a few bullet points. I am reserving the right to do a deeper dive on 2028 Senate races early in the new year, and we probably will do that. But I felt like I needed to give myself at least some rough, thin-sliced answers to the two questions posed by the subheadline. […]

tools.title: Models led prediction markets in forecasting the blue wave
tools.summary_raw: But who deserves the most credit? High-quality pollsters who nailed the result. Plus, Still Counting EP10.
tools.content_text: Our weekly episode of Still Counting is ready. This was taped yesterday morning, so you can blame any bad takes on sleep deprivation: And here’s the audio. We’re very grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes. Yes, I’m going to say that every week. The context Despite results on Tuesday that, to a first approximation, made our coverage this year look smart, Clare, Galen and I were all in slightly different moods. Elections build up to a stressful crescendo, frankly. It’s in the final days when you both have the most on the line and the most to do. Subscribe now And we’re still feeling that stress, to some extent. So rather than come up with the perfect transition paragraph, I’m going to semi-awkwardly pivot to a debate about models versus prediction markets. 1 I don’t particularly like this debate. To a large extent, I think of pollsters, modelers, prediction markets and smart political wonks as all being within “the industry”. Their interests are mostly aligned with one another. And sometimes they’re aligned against the conventional wisdom or the media ecosystem more broadly. If you’ve read the book, it’s kind of a Village vs. River thing. Or smart money vs. dumb money. The smart money was on Democrats having a good and possibly great election. The smart money doesn’t always get it right, though. Still, I’m finding myself a little annoyed if prediction markets are trying to take a disproportionate share of the credit as opposed to “the industry” broadly. A few key points. FLIPR was — correctly, given what happened — more confident in overall Democratic odds in the Senate throughout the stretch run of the campaign. 2 For the Nov. 3 datapoint in this chart, I’m using the last “print” of prediction market data before any results were reported starting at 6 p.m. There was a weird little jitter back toward Republicans at prediction markets during the course of the day on Tuesday, which was directionally wrong and I don’t think had any real basis, as I wrote at the time. Prediction markets are smart about incorporating new information, and in principle that’s one of their advantages versus models — we have to wait for whatever happens to show up in the polls. At the same time, there’s sometimes a “ buy the rumor, sell the news ” thing going on here. Markets almost certainly overreacted to the Haley Stevens thing in Michigan and to random reports about turnout on Tuesday morning and afternoon. Once results began to come in on Tuesday, prediction markets very, very quickly honed in on the right results. They were better than the networks, and faster than the NYT Needle. That was impressive, though I think we got to the right answer pretty quickly in the liveblog , too. However, if we are going to turn this into a competition, I think the better models like FLIPR unambiguously had a better pre-election period. Our model arrived at the right answer faster, leading the markets by days to weeks. […]

market.content_text: What a week! Recap it with the second edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading . The quiz will appear here through November as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck! 0 of 10 answered 1 of 10 Salon, one of the first digital-native news outlets, closed this week after 31 years. Which one of these journalists did not work at Salon at some point? Rebecca Traister Steve Kornacki Glenn Greenwald Jake Tapper Jonathan Chait “Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier,” the site wrote anonymously at its passing. Its last owner describes its core business as “Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto.” In The New York Times → 2 of 10 The AI lab Anthropic — the makers of Claude — recently signed its first licensing deal with a news publisher. Which publisher? The Wall Street Journal Bloomberg News The New York Times Associated Press Le Monde The deal was for real-time election results for Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. In Adweek → 3 of 10 Harassment by the Kremlin has forced Russia’s last major independent newspaper to close. Its editor won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. What is the newspaper’s name? Meduza Kommersant Novaya Gazeta The Moscow Times Nezavisimaya Gazeta Novaya Gazeta editor Dmitry Muratov in Moscow, Oct. 8, 2021. (AP/Alexander Zemlianichenko) “On November 9, we will ​turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave,” the paper said. “The newspaper no longer ​exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations.” In Reuters → 4 of 10 The New York Times brought back one of its most famous data visualizations, which debuted in 2016. What’s its name? The Syringe The Needle The Dart The Lance The Thorn The Needle scarred a generation of politics junkies with its constant jittering — and by giving Hillary Clinton an 82% chance of victory well into 2016’s election night. On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were...
market.content_text: Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users. On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 ★ Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Meta confirmed the indefinite delay in a statement to Nieman Lab. “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right,” said a spokesperson for the company. Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20. Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect. “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. market.content_text: The data is in : News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record , an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs. For Nikita Redkar , a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit. In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel. In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup. A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me. “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.” Four years into news content creation, Redkar has more than 943,000 TikTok followers, 674,000 Instagram followers, 33,000 YouTube subscribers , and 16,000 Substack subscribers. (Her handle on all of them is @nikitadumptruck.) She aims to explain issues in a way that’s funny and accessible — whether she’s attending protests outside the United Nations ( “Get ready with me to bully Netanyahu” ), traveling through Europe ( “Spend the day in socialist hellhole Denmark with me” ), or explaining the negative impacts of private equity companies ( “A private equity boyfriend is this summer’s hottest accessory” ). Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Hanaa’ Tameez : How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar : I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. […]

market.content_text: College football already has an Orange Bowl , a Peach Bowl , and a Citrus Bowl , so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl. But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl . Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion . (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million ; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator ; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd .) On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor ) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out : Some VERY big, fun news: The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game. Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl. A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas. But we've already been banned once. And we need your help. [image or embed] — Ben Collins ( @bencollins.bsky.social ) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it ). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month. This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription , a major driver of The Onion’s revenue. “We are a just a few thousand subscribers away from hitting 100,000 subscribers, which would catapult us above Jeff Bezos’ Washington Post in print circulation,” Collins wrote . “This would make us the 4th biggest newspaper in the United States. So we need more people to sign up before Christmas.” Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. […]
